strengths: First systematic attempt to apply hypergraph modeling and explicit high-order interaction (HOI) reasoning to audio deepfake detection (ADD), a domain that has predominantly relied on pairwise/local relational modules (attention, graph edges, convolutions).

The overall architecture is well-engineered: FCM-based soft hyperedge construction, a relational artifact amplification operator combining structural and feature-level self-similarity, and a class-aware prototype bank with EMA updates and a two-stage (soft/slot) alignment scheme for cross-batch consistency are all clearly described with equations.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 13 diverse test sets (different languages, codecs, spoofing methods, and 'in-the-wild' conditions), with consistent training-only-on-ASVspoof2019LA protocol, following the Speech DF Arena benchmark, which supports a reasonably standardized generalization study.

Multiple complementary analyses beyond aggregate EER/F1 numbers: hyperedge-cardinality distribution histograms, dataset-level clustermaps of relational similarity, PCA of prototype banks/aligned centroids, and sample-level segment analysis on PartialSpoof, which together provide some qualitative evidence that the learned hyperedges capture non-trivial multi-node relations rather than degenerating to pairwise edges.

Reasonably thorough ablations on sub-modules (amplification module, prototype banks, alignment algorithms) and on hyperedge count/degree hyperparameters, plus an additional ablation replacing AASIST's heterogeneous attention layer with the proposed HAGNN in a non-SSL setting, showing the idea is not entirely tied to one backbone.

Negative/mixed results (e.g., degradation on 2021LA and ASVspoof5, codec augmentation trade-offs) are reported rather than hidden, and the paper attempts to explain them via a channel-distortion hypothesis, which is a positive sign of honest reporting.
weaknesses: The central theoretical motivation (Section 3, O-information/synergy-dominated hypothesis) is never actually quantified on real ADD features: the paper introduces the C(Xn), B(Xn), Ω(Xn) formalism in detail but does not compute these quantities for actual embeddings from ASVspoof/other datasets to verify that ADD systems are indeed synergy-dominated (Ω<0). The claimed empirical support in Figure 1 (right) is instead just aggregated performance gains in Table 6, which is not evidence about the sign or magnitude of O-information; this leaves the theoretical framing largely rhetorical/post-hoc rather than empirically validated, undermining the 'first investigation of high-order effects...from an information-theoretic perspective' claim.

Inconsistent headline numbers: the abstract reports a 22.15% average relative gain across 11 datasets, while the conclusion states a 15.32% average relative gain across 13 datasets; this discrepancy is not explained and raises concerns about result reporting consistency/rigor.

Performance is inconsistent across benchmarks: HyperPotter underperforms its own baseline on ASVspoof2021LA and ASVspoof5 (Table 1), and the 'Strong Distortion' scenario in Table 6 also shows a decrease relative to baseline; the explanation ('channel interference masks HOIs') is speculative and not directly tested (e.g., no controlled experiment isolating distortion severity vs. Ω sign).

Several SOTA baselines in Table 1/5 have missing entries ('-') for many datasets, so the comparison to prior state-of-the-art is incomplete for many rows, making it hard to assess whether HyperPotter is truly SOTA across the full benchmark suite rather than only against its own retrained baseline.

No variance/statistical significance reporting: all results appear to be single-run numbers (no seeds, standard deviations, or significance tests), which is a concern given some of the EER differences (e.g., third-best vs baseline) are small and the method has many hyperparameters (β1, β2, τ, m, K, D, μ, γ, warm-start schedule) that could be tuned per-dataset.

The technical novelty is largely a recombination of existing techniques (Fuzzy C-Means clustering, hypergraph attention, EMA-based prototype memory, attention amplification) applied to a new domain, rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic contribution; the paper would benefit from more explicit justification of why this particular combination is necessary versus simpler high-order alternatives.

No analysis of computational overhead (training/inference time, FCM iteration cost) despite the added architectural complexity (multiple HAGNN layers, iterative FCM clustering, prototype bank maintenance), which matters for practical deployment claims.

The interpretive narrative in Sec 6.2 (positioning HyperPotter as a 'specialist' suited for MoE ensembles when it underperforms under channel distortion) reads as a post-hoc rationalization of weaknesses rather than a rigorously tested claim, and is not supported by any ensemble or MoE experiments in the paper.

strengths: The paper addresses an underexplored angle for audio deepfake detection (ADD) by proposing hypergraph-based modeling of high-order interactions (HOIs), which is a reasonable extension beyond pairwise graph/attention mechanisms used in prior ADD work.
The evaluation protocol is broad, covering 13 test sets that span different languages, codecs, and spoofing methods, which is commendable for assessing generalization.

The engineering design (FCM-based hyperedge construction, prototype bank with EMA updates, relational artifact amplification) is described in reasonable technical detail, and an extensive set of ablations (sub-modules, alignment strategies, hyperedge count/degree, codec augmentation) is provided.

Some interpretability visualizations (hyperedge cardinality distributions, dataset clustering, PCA of prototypes, sample-level segment analysis on PartialSpoof) are included to support the qualitative claim that HOIs are captured.
weaknesses: The paper's central intellectual claim — that ADD artifacts are dominated by synergistic (as opposed to redundant) high-order interactions, justified via O-information theory — is never actually verified quantitatively on real ADD features. Section 3 only presents the theoretical formalism and qualitative reasoning; the authors explicitly admit 'a rigorous quantification of the synergy in ADD remains an open problem.' The supposed empirical support in Figure 1 (right panel) is circular: it merely shows HyperPotter (the proposed method) outperforming the pairwise baseline, which does not constitute independent evidence for the O-information hypothesis motivating the method's design.

Key summary numbers are inconsistent across the paper: the abstract claims a 22.15% average relative gain across 11 datasets, while the conclusion states 15.32% across 13 datasets, with no reconciliation of these figures or clear description of how they were computed, undermining confidence in the reported headline results.

Empirical results are mixed and not uniformly supportive of the method: HyperPotter underperforms the baseline on ASVspoof2021LA and ASVspoof5 (channel-distorted conditions), and the explanation ('distortions act as masks that obscure HOIs') is a post-hoc narrative not independently tested or verified.

Comparisons with SOTA baselines in Table 1 have many missing entries (dashes) for several models/datasets, making it hard to assess whether HyperPotter's advantage generalizes fairly against those methods on the same conditions; the 13.96% cross-domain SOTA gain is computed over only 4 selected datasets, raising concern about selective reporting.

No variance/statistical significance information is reported; experiments appear to use a single fixed random seed (1234), which is concerning given the paper reports fine-grained EER differences (e.g., <1 point) across many datasets as evidence of improvement or degradation.

The reproducibility statement leaves the code repository URL blank ('The code and pre-trained models are available at .'), and several implementation choices (e.g., FCM iteration details, warm-start schedule, similarity gate decay) are numerous and finely tuned, raising reproducibility concerns absent released code.

The novelty of 'hyperedges' as FCM soft-clustering outputs is somewhat overstated; the 'degree-free hypergraph' formulation (each hyperedge connects all nodes with varying membership) is a nonstandard use of hypergraph terminology and is closer to soft-clustering-based attention pooling than a conventional hypergraph with sparse multi-way edges, which weakens the claimed conceptual novelty relative to prior hypergraph literature (e.g., LHGNN, ViHGNN) that is not empirically compared as a baseline.

Added parameters are minimal (0.03M) yet the method introduces nontrivial computational overhead (iterative FCM clustering per sample, EMA-based prototype updates, additional attention modules); no runtime/inference latency or training time comparison is provided, leaving practical cost unclear.

Ablation tables (e.g., Table 3) show inconsistent trends across datasets without a single clearly justified default configuration, and some conclusions drawn from the tables (e.g., 'D=2 reduces the hypergraph to a pairwise graph and leads to performance degradation') are only partially supported by the presented numbers.

Minor presentation issues, including a typo in the section title ('Hypergragh-based Detection Framework'), dense and occasionally unclear figures/tables, and terminology that shifts between sections (e.g., use of 'high-order interactions' vs. specific FCM cluster mechanics) reduce overall clarity.

strengths: Novel problem framing: the paper is the first to explicitly investigate high-order interactions (HOIs) in audio deepfake detection, motivated by O-information theory distinguishing redundant vs. synergistic multivariate dependencies, offering a fresh conceptual lens beyond the standard local/pairwise (CNN/attention/graph) paradigm.

Technically well-developed framework: HyperPotter combines FCM-based soft hyperedge construction, an attention-driven relational artifact amplification operator (fusing structural and feature-level self-similarity), and a class-aware prototype bank with a principled two-stage (soft/slot) alignment and EMA update scheme for cross-batch memory, which is a reasonably sophisticated and self-consistent design.

Extensive empirical evaluation: experiments span 13 diverse test sets (cross-lingual, cross-codec, varied attacks/speakers), with EER and F1 metrics, comparisons against ~10 recent SOTA baselines, and thorough ablations (sub-modules, alignment algorithms, hyperedge count/degree, codec augmentation, SSL-free backbone).

Good reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, training procedure, augmentation strategies, hardware, and dataset descriptions are provided in the appendix, and the paper commits to releasing code/checkpoints.

Insightful qualitative analyses: hyperedge cardinality distributions, dataset clustering by relational similarity, PCA of prototype banks, and sample/segment-level visualizations on PartialSpoof provide some interpretability into what the hypergraph structure is capturing.

Parameter efficiency: gains are achieved with only ~0.03M additional parameters relative to the strong Wav2Vec2-AASIST baseline, suggesting the architectural change (not just capacity) drives improvements.
weaknesses: The central theoretical motivation (O-information/synergy analysis) is never actually computed on the paper's own ADD features/embeddings to verify the core hypothesis; the paper explicitly admits 'a rigorous quantification of the synergy in ADD remains an open problem,' making the connection between the theory in Section 3 and the proposed architecture largely qualitative/motivational rather than empirically validated, weakening the claimed causal link between O-information theory and the design choices.

Inconsistent overall performance: HyperPotter underperforms the baseline on ASVspoof2021LA and ASVspoof5 (heavily codec/distortion-affected sets), and the explanation given (distortions 'mask' HOIs, positioning the model as a 'specialist') reads as post-hoc rationalization rather than a rigorously supported claim; Table 6 also shows a clear drop in the 'Strong Distortion' scenario.

Reported headline numbers are inconsistent across the paper: the abstract states a 22.15% average relative gain and 13.96% improvement over SOTA on 4 cross-domain sets, while the conclusion states a 15.32% average relative gain — this discrepancy is not explained and raises concerns about the care taken in reporting aggregate statistics.

No error bars, multiple random seeds, or significance testing are reported anywhere; given that many EER gaps (e.g., 21DF baseline vs. HyperPotter, or third-best entries) are small, it is unclear whether the observed improvements are statistically meaningful versus run-to-run variance.

The SOTA comparison table (Table 1) has substantial missing entries ('-') for many baselines/datasets, since prior papers were not evaluated on all 13 sets; this makes some of the 'best/second-best' claims only partially comparable across methods.

The prototype bank mechanism introduces many additional hyperparameters (τ, µ, γ, warm-start epoch schedule, alignment stage transition epochs) without a systematic sensitivity analysis, raising concerns about robustness/tuning burden and potential overfitting to the specific ASVspoof2019LA training protocol.

The auxiliary ablation replacing AASIST's graph attention with HAGNN (Table 8, Appendix H) uses a much weaker non-SSL backbone and shows mixed/inconsistent results (e.g., degradation on 19LA), which is not well integrated into the main narrative and slightly undercuts the claimed generality of the HOI benefit.

The paper builds heavily on an existing strong backbone (Wav2Vec2-AASIST) and known techniques (FCM clustering, EMA prototypes, hypergraph attention), so while the combination and application to ADD is novel, the individual technical components are largely adaptations of existing methods rather than fundamentally new mechanisms.

strengths: Novel framing of audio deepfake detection through the lens of high-order interactions (HOIs) and O-information theory, providing a fresh conceptual angle relative to the dominant pairwise/graph-attention paradigm in ADD.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: 13 cross-scenario test sets, comparisons with numerous recent SOTA methods, thorough ablations (sub-modules, alignment algorithms, hyperedge count/cardinality, FCM iterations), stability across seeds, scalability to longer audio, and detailed computational cost analysis (latency/throughput/VRAM) in the appendix.

Honest and detailed limitations discussion: the paper explicitly identifies and analyzes degradation under codec/channel distortion (21LA, ASVspoof5), rather than hiding negative results, and explores augmentation remedies.

Reasonable reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, pseudocode for the hypergraph attention layer, dataset descriptions, and development-set robustness checks (Appendix B.2) that test sensitivity of checkpoint selection to different dev sets.

Interesting diagnostic visualizations (O-information heatmaps, hyperedge cardinality distributions, PCA of prototype banks, sample-level segment analysis) that offer some qualitative support for the high-order relational modeling claim.
weaknesses: The connection between the O-information theoretical motivation (Section 3) and the actual method (Sections 4-5) is loose: the FCM/hypergraph/prototype architecture is not derived from or optimized to explicitly increase synergy or O-information; the O-information analysis is a post-hoc diagnostic overlay rather than an integral part of the training objective, and the authors themselves concede they are not offering "a formal decomposition into pure redundancy or pure synergy," weakening the causal story linking theory to design choices.

Performance gains are inconsistent: the method underperforms the baseline on 2 of 13 sets (21LA, ASVspoof5) and ablations show that removing key modules (amplification, prototypes) sometimes *improves* results on these same codec-heavy sets, suggesting the architecture is not clearly principled but rather empirically tuned to the majority of test conditions, undermining the generality of the core "HOI is important" claim.

Non-trivial computational overhead: Table 13 shows roughly 3-4x higher per-sample latency and substantially lower throughput than the baseline across batch sizes, which is a significant practical cost for a method whose average relative EER reduction (12.68%) is meaningful but not transformative, especially given failure cases under distortion that are common in real deployment (telephony/codec channels).

Many architectural hyperparameters (β1, β2, warm-start epoch schedule, similarity gate decay, slot/soft alignment epoch boundaries) appear to be manually fixed based on "early model design" without systematic justification, raising concerns about overfitting to the specific benchmark suite and limiting confidence in generalizability to new settings.

The novelty is primarily an engineering combination of existing techniques (FCM soft clustering, hypergraph attention, prototype-guided initialization borrowed from domain adaptation/incremental learning) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic or theoretical contribution; the claimed "first investigation of HOI in ADD via O-information" is more of a novel analytical framing than a rigorously validated new mechanism.

Some result tables have missing baseline entries (dashes) making several cross-method comparisons incomplete, and reported baseline numbers sometimes diverge from other published results, which could reflect reproduction variance not fully discussed in the main text.

strengths: First systematic exploration of high-order interaction (hypergraph) modeling for audio deepfake detection, motivated by an information-theoretic (O-information) perspective that is conceptually interesting and underexplored in this domain.

Very extensive empirical evaluation across 13 (and additional supplementary) test sets spanning diverse languages, codecs, attack types, and speaker conditions, going well beyond typical ADD papers in scope.

Thorough supplementary analysis including ablations on sub-modules, hyperedge count/cardinality sensitivity, random-seed stability, scalability to longer audio, computational complexity/cost breakdown, and sample-level qualitative visualizations (PCA, clustermaps).
Honest and detailed discussion of limitations under severe codec/channel distortion rather than only reporting favorable results.

Reasonably novel architectural components (FCM-based soft hyperedges, prototype-guided initialization with class-aware banks and EMA updates, attention-driven relational amplification) that are described with sufficient mathematical detail for partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central information-theoretic motivation (synergy-dominated HOIs driving generalizable artifacts) is never rigorously quantified for the ADD task itself; the paper explicitly concedes 'a rigorous quantification of the synergy in ADD remains an open problem,' making Section 3 largely a qualitative narrative rather than an evidence-based derivation of the method, and the O-information analysis in Fig. 3/Appendix B.3 is post-hoc and interpretive rather than a validated diagnostic that predicts where/why HyperPotter should help.

Performance gains are inconsistent and often modest: HyperPotter underperforms the retrained baseline on 2/13 sets (21LA, ASVspoof5) and is frequently not competitive with prior SOTA methods on individual datasets (e.g., Table 1 shows several existing methods achieving markedly lower EER on 19LA, 21LA, 21DF, FoR). The headline '13.96% EER reduction on 4 challenging datasets' and 'average relative EER reduction' statistics appear to selectively emphasize favorable subsets.

Substantial computational overhead for the reported gains: Table 13 shows ~4x higher inference latency and much lower throughput than the baseline (e.g., 77.5ms vs 19.5ms per-sample latache, 12.9 vs 51.4 utt/s at batch size 1), which is a serious practical concern for an anti-spoofing system intended for real-time or large-scale deployment, yet this trade-off is not adequately weighed against the marginal/mixed accuracy improvements.

The framework has many interacting design choices (FCM fuzzifier, iteration count, hyperedge count K, cardinality R, similarity gate schedule, two-stage soft/slot alignment, EMA momentum, fusion weights β1/β2) most of which were tuned or fixed by informal heuristics per Appendix B.1 ('chosen during early model design and kept fixed'); combined with the ablation Table 3 showing opposite trends across datasets for the same hyperparameter, this raises concern that reported gains may partly reflect hyperparameter/checkpoint selection idiosyncrasies rather than a robust, principled effect of HOI modeling.

Checkpoint selection uses a subset of the In-the-Wild test set as a de facto validation set, and the authors acknowledge this does not correspond to the best hyperparameter configuration for that very test set; while Appendix B.2 attempts to address fairness with alternate dev sets, the practice of tuning near a reported test set is methodologically questionable and the alternate-dev-set results still show non-trivial fluctuation in relative gains.

Non-uniform, sometimes contradictory benefits from core components under codec-heavy conditions (e.g., Table 2 shows removing the amplification module or prototype banks improves EER on 21LA/ASVspoof5), undermining the claim that the proposed synergistic HOI mechanisms are uniformly beneficial or well understood, and weakening the paper's central thesis.
Code/pretrained model link is left as a placeholder ('available at .'), so full reproducibility cannot currently be verified despite the detailed pseudocode.

strengths: Novel problem framing: the paper is the first to systematically motivate audio deepfake detection (ADD) via high-order interactions (HOIs) and to ground this motivation with a principled information-theoretic tool (O-information), providing an interesting conceptual bridge between redundancy/synergy theory and hypergraph-based ADD modeling.

The proposed HyperPotter architecture is reasonably well engineered, combining FCM-based soft hyperedge construction, an attention-driven relational artifact amplification module, and a class-aware prototype bank with EMA updates and soft/slot alignment for cross-batch consistency.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 13 cross-scenario test sets covering different languages, codecs, and spoofing methods, plus substantial appendix material (F1 scores, additional datasets such as EmoFake/MLAAD/SingFake, scalability to 8s audio, stability across three random seeds, sensitivity to hyperparameters K/R/T, and detailed complexity/latency/VRAM analysis).

Honest and detailed limitations discussion: the paper explicitly identifies and analyzes degraded performance under severe codec/channel distortion (21LA, ASVspoof5) rather than hiding it, and offers a plausible explanation (distortion masking fine-grained relational structure).

Good ablation coverage isolating the amplification module, prototype banks, and the two alignment algorithms, as well as hyperedge count/cardinality sweeps, which helps substantiate (to some extent) the necessity of HOI modeling over pure pairwise mechanisms.

Rich qualitative and quantitative interpretability analysis (O-information heatmaps, hyperedge cardinality distributions, dataset/sample-level clustering, PCA of prototype banks) that gives some insight into what the hypergraph module is learning.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim (that ADD artifacts are predominantly synergy-dominated and hypergraphs capture this better than pairwise graphs) is only supported by suggestive, qualitative O-information visualizations (Fig. 3) on learned centroids; the authors themselves concede this is not a rigorous decomposition, weakening the causal link between the theoretical motivation and the proposed architecture.

Gains are inconsistent across several important, non-trivial evaluation sets (2021LA, ASVspoof5, and some ADD tracks show performance degradation relative to baseline), and the ablations show that removing the amplification module or prototype banks actually improves results on 21LA/ASVspoof5 in some configurations — this undercuts the generality of the core claim that HOI modeling is broadly beneficial.

Substantial added computational cost: Table 13 shows roughly 3-4x higher per-batch inference/training latency and markedly lower throughput than the baseline for only a modest average EER improvement, which limits the practical significance of the method, especially since the paper does not compare this added cost against other competitive SOTA baselines.

The checkpoint/model-selection protocol uses a held-out subset of the In-the-Wild (ITW) dataset for early stopping, while ITW itself is one of the headline test sets reported in the main comparison table; although the paper attempts to address this with alternative dev-set reruns (Appendix B.2), the practice of tuning against a dataset that doubles as a primary reported benchmark raises fairness/leakage concerns relative to baselines that do not use such tailored selection.

The framework has many heuristically chosen design elements (similarity gate schedule, 20%/80% prototype slot allocation, specific epoch thresholds for switching alignment strategies, fusion weights β1/β2) whose individual necessity is not fully justified via ablation, raising concerns about overfitting to the specific benchmark suite and about reproducibility of these choices in new settings.

Baseline SOTA comparisons in Table 1 mix self-reproduced results with numbers copied from original papers under potentially different training/evaluation protocols, which can introduce inconsistencies that are hard for readers to control for when judging the significance of the reported improvements.
